pos: n. (the Breton capital and see, seat of the parlement of Brittany, largely rebuilt after the fire of 1720)
etymology: From the Gaulish tribe the Redones, through Latin Redonis; the Breton form is Roazhon.
biblical_def: Rennes at the confluence of the Ille and the Vilaine was the capital of Brittany and a see from the fourth century. After the union of Brittany with France it became the seat of the provincial parlement, whose lawyers and officeholders gave the city its character; the parlement resisted royal taxation repeatedly and was exiled from the city for its pains. In December 1720 a fire that began in a carpenter's shop burned for a week and destroyed some nine hundred timber houses in the heart of the town, which was rebuilt to a regular plan in granite — the reason Rennes has a classical centre inside a medieval street pattern. The dictionary records Rennes for the rebuilding, and for what a city does after it loses almost everything. The plan adopted was more orderly than what burned. Scripture does not promise that the second house will be plainer, and in one famous case promises the contrary: “The glory of this latter house shall be greater than of the former, saith the LORD of hosts” (Hag 2:9). The prayer that fits a people clearing ash is “establish thou the work of our hands upon us” (Psa 90:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a parlement is given under parliament as a supreme council; a conflagration as a great fire; granite as a hard stone of crystalline texture; to rebuild as to build again; and glory as honour or splendour.
webster_full: PARLIAMENT, n. The supreme legislature of Great Britain; in France, formerly, the highest court of judicature.
CONFLAGRATION, n. A great fire, or the burning of any great mass of combustibles, as a house or a city.
GRANITE, n. A stone composed of feldspar, quartz and mica, of a crystalline texture and of great hardness.
REBUILD, v.t. To build again; to renew a structure; to build or construct what has been demolished.
GLORY, n. Brightness; luster; splendor; honor; praise; celebrity.
scriptures: Hag 2:9
The glory of this latter house shall be greater than of the former, saith the LORD of hosts: and in this place will I give peace, saith the LORD of hosts.
And let the beauty of the LORD our God be upon us: and establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it.
Zec 4:6
Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the LORD unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.
Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.
corruption_summary: Breton capital and see, seat of the provincial parlement, rebuilt in granite to a regular plan after the fire of December 1720.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's rebuilding is not always a reduction. Haggai's word to men looking at a poorer temple is “The glory of this latter house shall be greater than of the former, saith the LORD of hosts” (Hag 2:9), which is a promise and not a consolation. A city rebuilt better after a fire is a faint picture of it.

The live temptation is to credit the recovery to the planners. Zechariah spoke over a rebuilding and excluded that accounting, “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6). The Psalmist asks instead for the work of our hands to be established, “establish thou the work of our hands upon us” (Psa 90:17), and Paul attaches the promise to the labour itself, “your labour is not in vain in the Lord” (1Co 15:58).

pos: n. (the Cornouaille see in Brittany whose cathedral nave is visibly out of line with its choir)
etymology: Breton kemper, a confluence, where the Steir meets the Odet.
biblical_def: Quimper in western Brittany is the see of Cornouaille, named for the confluence of its two rivers, and its cathedral of St Corentin has a peculiarity known to every student of Gothic: the thirteenth-century choir and the fifteenth-century nave do not line up. The nave swings several degrees off the choir's axis, a deflection of some five feet, forced by the ground and the older chapel the builders would not demolish. Masons dressed the junction as best they could, and the bend is plainly visible from either end. The dictionary records Quimper for that bend, because it is an unusually honest building. The deviation was not hidden; it was accommodated and left in view, and anybody walking the length of the church can see where the compromise was made. That is the better way with a fault. Scripture asks for a straight handling of the text, “Study to shew thyself approved unto God” (2Ti 2:15), whose verb is a word for cutting straight, and “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” (1Th 5:21) keeps the measuring going rather than declaring the job finished.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an axis as a straight line through a body; a deflection as a turning aside; a nave as the body of a church; oblique as deviating from a right line; and rectitude as uprightness.
webster_full: AXIS, n. The straight line, real or imaginary, passing through a body, on which it revolves, or may revolve.
DEFLECTION, n. Deviation; a turning aside; a turning or bending from a right line or regular course.
NAVE, n. The middle or body of a church, extending from the baluster or rail of the altar to the chief door.
OBLIQUE, a. Deviating from a right line; not direct; not perpendicular; not parallel.
RECTITUDE, n. Uprightness; rightness of principle or practice; exact conformity to truth.
scriptures: Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
Jer 6:16
Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein.
corruption_summary: Breton see whose cathedral nave deflects several degrees from the axis of its older choir, the junction left visible.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is honesty about a crooked joint. Quimper's masons could not straighten the axis and did not pretend to; the bend is there to be seen. Paul's word for handling Scripture is a word about cutting straight, “Study to shew thyself approved unto God” (2Ti 2:15), and it assumes the workman knows where his line runs.

The live temptation is to treat an accommodation as a principle, so that the bend becomes the plan. Scripture keeps the measuring open, “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” (1Th 5:21), and asks for arrangements that serve the congregation, “Let all things be done decently and in order.” (1Co 14:40). Jeremiah's remedy for a drifted course is to ask after the original line, “Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein” (Jer 6:16).

pos: n. (the Morbihan see of the council of about 465, where Vincent Ferrer died in 1419)
etymology: From the Gaulish tribe the Veneti, through Latin Venetis; the Breton form is Gwened.
biblical_def: Vannes on the Gulf of Morbihan was the city of the Veneti whom Caesar defeated at sea, and a see from the fifth century. A council held there about 465 issued canons on clerical discipline that were long cited, and the Breton estates met in the town repeatedly; the union of Brittany with France was ratified there in 1532. Vannes was also where Vincent Ferrer, the Valencian Dominican who spent his last years preaching through Brittany, died in 1419 and was buried in the cathedral. The dictionary records Vannes for Ferrer, because he is the late medieval preacher at his most impressive and most dangerous. He drew enormous crowds, preached repentance and the nearness of judgment, and also preached against the Jews of Spain with consequences that ran to forced conversion. The lesson is that fervour is not the test. “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” (1Th 5:21) is applied to preachers as to anyone, and “speak thou the things which become sound doctrine” (Tit 2:1) asks what was actually said, while “it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe” (1Co 1:21) locates the power in the message rather than the crowd.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a canon as a law of the church; a preacher as one who discourses publicly on religious subjects; fervour as heat of mind; a multitude as a great number; and conversion as a change of heart.
webster_full: CANON, n. In ecclesiastical affairs, a law or rule of doctrine or discipline enacted by a council.
PREACHER, n. One who discourses publicly on religious subjects; one who inculcates any thing with earnestness.
FERVOR, n. Heat or warmth; ardor of mind; animated or intense feeling; zeal.
MULTITUDE, n. A great number, indefinitely; a crowd or throng; the populace.
CONVERSION, n. In a theological or moral sense, a change of heart, or dispositions, in which the enmity of the heart to God is subdued.
scriptures: Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
Tit 2:1
But speak thou the things which become sound doctrine:
For after that in the wisdom of God the world by wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe.
Zec 4:6
Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the LORD unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.
corruption_summary: Morbihan see of the council of c. 465, burial place of the preacher Vincent Ferrer, who died there in 1419.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a crowd is not a verdict. Ferrer drew multitudes and some of what he preached was poison, and Paul gives the congregation the same instrument it always has: “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” (1Th 5:21). The question put to any preacher is content, “speak thou the things which become sound doctrine” (Tit 2:1).

The live temptation is to measure a ministry by its effects, which was precisely how Ferrer's was defended. Scripture puts the power in the message and not the response, “it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe” (1Co 1:21), and Zechariah rules out the kind of pressure that produced forced conversions in Spain: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6).

pos: n. (the Burgundian see of Germanus, who was sent to Britain against Pelagianism in 429)
etymology: From Latin Autissiodurum, heavily contracted in French; the x is not sounded.
biblical_def: Auxerre on the Yonne was a see from the third century, and its most consequential bishop was Germanus, who held it from 418 until 448. In 429 he was sent to Britain, with Lupus of Troyes, to confront the Pelagian teaching that had taken hold there, and the mission is recorded by Prosper and by Constantius' life of Germanus; a second visit followed about 447. Patrick was by one tradition trained under him at Auxerre before going to Ireland. The cathedral school later produced the Carolingian commentators Haimo and Remigius of Auxerre. The dictionary records Auxerre for the 429 mission, because Pelagianism is the error the Reformed churches have always regarded as the deepest, and Germanus crossed the sea to answer it. That a man can contribute to his own salvation by unaided will is excluded by the sentence Augustine pressed and the Reformers recovered: “by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves” (Eph 2:8), with “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9) closing it, and “not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law” (Phi 3:9) renouncing the alternative in the first person.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Pelagianism as the doctrines of Pelagius, who denied original sin; free will as the power of choosing; original sin as the corruption derived from Adam; grace as the free favour of God; and a mission as a sending forth.
webster_full: PELAGIAN, n. A follower of Pelagius, a monk, who denied original sin and the doctrines of grace.
FREE-WILL, n. The power of directing our own actions without constraint by necessity or fate.
SIN, n. The voluntary departure of a moral agent from a known rule of rectitude or duty, prescribed by God.
GRACE, n. The free unmerited love and favour of God, the spring and source of all the benefits men receive from him.
MISSION, n. A sending or delegating; persons sent; commission; the act of sending.
scriptures: Eph 2:8
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Eph 2:9
Not of works, lest any man should boast.
Phi 3:9
And be found in him, not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith:
Rom 3:28
Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law.
corruption_summary: Burgundian see whose bishop Germanus was sent to Britain in 429 to confront Pelagianism, and whose school produced the Carolingian commentators.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is why Pelagianism matters enough to cross a sea for. If a man can turn himself to God unaided, the gospel is advice; Paul's sentence makes it a gift, “by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves” (Eph 2:8), and forecloses the alternative at once, “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9).

The live temptation is a soft form of the same error that keeps grace as a word and lets merit back in through the side door. Paul refuses it in the first person, “not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law” (Phi 3:9), which is the most personal statement of the doctrine in Scripture. The conclusion he draws is flat: “a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law” (Rom 3:28).

pos: n. (the Champagne see where Rashi taught, and where the Templar rule was approved in 1129)
etymology: From the Gaulish tribe the Tricasses, through Latin Tricassium; the final consonants are silent.
biblical_def: Troyes in Champagne was a see from the third century, a great fair town whose weight standard survives in the troy ounce, and the place where the Council of Troyes in 1129 approved the rule of the Knights Templar at Bernard of Clairvaux's urging. Its deepest importance for the history of Bible reading is a school of a different kind. Rashi, Solomon ben Isaac, lived and taught at Troyes from about 1040 until 1105 and wrote there his commentaries on the Hebrew Bible and the Talmud, insisting throughout on the plain sense of the words. Nicholas of Lyra drew heavily on Rashi in the fourteenth century, Luther used Lyra, and the literal reading that the Reformation made its method reaches back in part through Troyes. The dictionary records Troyes for that line of descent, with the credit stated plainly. “Thy word is true from the beginning” (Psa 119:160) is the Psalmist's claim for the words themselves, and “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.” (Psa 119:130) the ground for reading them as they stand.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the literal sense as that according to the letter; a commentary as an exposition; Hebrew as the language of the Hebrews; exegesis is given under exposition as explanation; and plain as evident to the understanding.
webster_full: LITERAL, a. According to the letter; primitive; real; not figurative or metaphorical.
COMMENTARY, n. A comment; exposition; explanation; illustration of difficult and obscure passages in an author.
HEBREW, n. A Jew; the language of the Hebrews; one of the Shemitic family of languages.
EXPOSITION, n. A laying open; a setting to public view; explanation; interpretation.
PLAIN, a. Evident to the understanding; clear; manifest; not obscure or difficult to be understood.
scriptures: Thy word is true from the beginning: and every one of thy righteous judgments endureth for ever.
The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
corruption_summary: Champagne see and fair town where Rashi taught from about 1040, whose literal exegesis reached the Reformation through Nicholas of Lyra.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the plain sense, and the credit for insisting on it where credit is due. Rashi at Troyes held the words to mean what they say, and the Psalmist makes the same claim for them, “Thy word is true from the beginning” (Psa 119:160). The benefit promised is to the ordinary reader, “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.” (Psa 119:130).

The live temptation is allegory that frees a reader from the text, which the medieval fourfold method encouraged and which the Reformers cut away. The claim is made for the writing itself, “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16), and the model reader checks the preacher against it, “searched the scriptures daily” (Act 17:11) — impossible if the meaning floats free of the letter.

pos: n. (the Champagne see on its plateau, whose bishop ranked as a duke and peer of France)
etymology: From the Gaulish tribe the Lingones, through Latin Lingonis.
biblical_def: Langres stands on a long promontory above the sources of the Marne and the Aube, a Roman town whose walls still ring the old city, and a see from the second century. Its bishops held the rank of duke and peer of France and were among the six ecclesiastical peers who attended the coronation at Reims, exercising temporal lordship over a substantial territory. Denis Diderot was born there in 1713, the son of a cutler, and was sent to the Jesuits before he went to Paris. The dictionary records Langres for the bishop-dukes, because the title states a problem the Reformation addressed directly. A bishop who is also a duke has two masters and two sets of interests, and the New Testament's description of his office contains nothing a duke needs. “Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock” (Act 20:28) is the whole of his charge, and “he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts” (Mal 2:7) is his dignity: a man carrying knowledge. “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6) removes the sword from the business entirely.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a peer as a nobleman; temporal as pertaining to this life, secular; a lordship as dominion; investiture as the act of giving possession; and an overseer as one who superintends.
webster_full: PEER, n. An equal; one of the same rank; a nobleman; as a peer of the realm.
TEMPORAL, a. Pertaining to this life or this world; secular, as opposed to spiritual or ecclesiastical.
LORDSHIP, n. The state or quality of being a lord; dominion; power; authority.
INVESTITURE, n. The act of giving possession of a manor, office or benefice.
OVERSEER, n. One who overlooks; a superintendent; a supervisor.
scriptures: Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
Mal 2:7
For the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth: for he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts.
Zec 4:6
Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the LORD unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.
Jam 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
corruption_summary: Champagne see whose bishops ranked as dukes and peers of France, with temporal lordship and a seat at the coronation.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the content of the office. Paul tells the elders what they are for in a single clause, “Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock” (Act 20:28), and Malachi gives the only dignity attached to it, “he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts” (Mal 2:7). Neither requires a duchy.

The live temptation is to suppose temporal power lets a bishop do more good. Zechariah settles the question for any work of God, “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6). And the measure of a churchman's religion is not his rank but James' test, “To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world” (Jam 1:27), which a peer of France is as free to fail as anyone.

pos: n. (the Franche-Comte archbishopric, holder of a shroud relic destroyed in 1794)
etymology: From the Gaulish Vesontio, through Latin; the French form carries a cedilla not reproduced in the slug.
biblical_def: Besancon, in a loop of the Doubs beneath a great citadel, was the metropolitan see of Franche-Comte and an imperial free city before its conquest by Louis XIV in 1674. Its archbishops included Antoine Perrenot de Granvelle, the minister of Charles V and Philip II in the Netherlands whose policies helped provoke the Dutch revolt. The cathedral of St Jean held from the sixteenth century a shroud venerated as the burial cloth of Christ, a rival to the better-known cloth at Chambery and then Turin; the Besancon shroud was examined under the Revolution, declared a painted linen, and destroyed in 1794. The dictionary records Besancon beside Hailes and Fecamp as the third relic in this group to fail an examination. The pattern is the argument. Where these objects were tested they did not survive the test, and the doctrine never depended on the outcome: “by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves” (Eph 2:8) and “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9) leave a shroud nothing to do, and “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” (1Th 5:21) is the duty that each of these cases shows unperformed for centuries.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a shroud as the dress of the dead; linen as cloth made of flax; a metropolitan as an archbishop; to venerate as to regard with reverence; and examination as a search for truth by questions.
webster_full: SHROUD, n. The dress of the dead; a winding sheet.
LINEN, n. Cloth made of flax or hemp.
METROPOLITAN, n. The bishop of a mother church; an archbishop.
VENERATE, v.t. To regard with respect and reverence; to reverence; to revere.
EXAMINATION, n. A careful search or inquiry, with a view to discover truth; a careful and accurate inspection.

corruption_summary: Franche-Comte archbishopric whose venerated shroud was examined under the Revolution, found to be a painted linen, and destroyed in 1794.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the doctrine was never hostage to the relic. Besancon's shroud failed an examination as Hailes' phial did, and the gospel is unaffected either way: “by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves” (Eph 2:8), with “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9) shutting out the whole economy of objects.

The live temptation is to make the argument turn on authentication, as though a genuine shroud would have justified the cult. It would not. Christ fixes worship in spirit and truth, “God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.” (Joh 4:24), and Paul assigns the examination that centuries of veneration never conducted: “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” (1Th 5:21).

pos: n. (the first Roman colony in Gaul, Visigothic capital and archbishopric, with an unfinished cathedral)
etymology: From Latin Narbo Martius, the colony founded in 118 BC; the province of Narbonensis took its name.
biblical_def: Narbonne was founded in 118 BC as the first Roman colony in Gaul and gave its name to the province of Narbonensis. It was the capital of the Visigothic kingdom in Septimania, a great Mediterranean port until its river silted and shifted, and an archbishopric whose province covered much of Languedoc. Its cathedral of St Just was begun in 1272 on an ambitious scale and never finished: the choir was built to a vault well over a hundred feet, and the nave was abandoned because completing it required breaching the Roman city wall, which the consuls refused to allow. The choir stands alone, like the choir at Beauvais. The dictionary records Narbonne for the wall and the choir, because the two make an unexpectedly exact figure. The church could not grow without taking down a defence the city believed it needed. Scripture turns that around: the wall is not an obstacle to the church but an image of it, “I have set watchmen upon thy walls, O Jerusalem” (Isa 62:6), and the only foundation that matters is already laid, “other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1Co 3:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a colony as a body of people in a new country; a rampart as an elevation of earth round a place; a choir as the part of a church where the singers are; unfinished as incomplete; and a watchman as one who guards.
webster_full: COLONY, n. A company or body of people transplanted from their mother country to a remote province or country.
RAMPART, n. In fortification, an elevation or mound of earth round a place, capable of resisting the cannon of an enemy.
CHOIR, n. A band or collection of singers; the part of a church appropriated to the singers.
UNFINISHED, a. Not complete; imperfect; not brought to an end; left in an incomplete state.
WATCHMAN, n. A sentinel; a guard; one who keeps watch, especially in the night.
scriptures: Isa 62:6
I have set watchmen upon thy walls, O Jerusalem, which shall never hold their peace day nor night: ye that make mention of the LORD, keep not silence,
For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ.
For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?
Psa 11:3
If the foundations be destroyed, what can the righteous do?
corruption_summary: First Roman colony in Gaul and Languedoc archbishopric, whose cathedral nave was abandoned rather than breach the Roman city wall.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the church is not in competition with a city's walls. Narbonne stopped building rather than breach its rampart, and Isaiah uses the wall as the picture of the ministry itself, “I have set watchmen upon thy walls, O Jerusalem” (Isa 62:6) — men set on it who do not keep silence.

The live temptation is to measure a church by what it managed to build. The foundation is not a matter of masonry at all, “other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1Co 3:11). Christ asks the builder to reckon first, “intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost” (Luk 14:28), and the Psalmist asks the question that outlives every unfinished nave, “If the foundations be destroyed, what can the righteous do?” (Psa 11:3).

pos: n. (the Languedoc see that named the Albigensians, with its fortress cathedral of brick)
etymology: From Latin Albiga; the Cathars of Languedoc were called Albigenses from the town, though it was not their centre.
biblical_def: Albi on the Tarn gave its name to the Albigensians, the Cathars of Languedoc, although the sect was never concentrated there. The Cathars taught a dualism of two principles, a good God of spirit and an evil creator of matter, denied the incarnation and the resurrection of the body, rejected the Old Testament, and divided believers into a perfect few and a mass of adherents. Innocent III proclaimed a crusade against them in 1209; it ran for twenty years under Simon de Montfort and his successors, destroyed the independent culture of Languedoc, and produced the massacre at Beziers and the burnings at Montsegur. Albi's answer was built in brick: the cathedral of Ste Cecile, begun in 1282, a windowless-looking fortress church raised as a statement of restored authority. The dictionary records Albi with both judgements, because only both are honest. The Cathars were not Protestant forebears and their doctrine fails the test of “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16), which includes the books they threw out. And the crusade against them fails “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6) and “ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free” (Joh 8:32) equally.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a Cathar is given under Catharist as one of a sect; dualism is given under dualist as one who maintains two principles; a crusade as a holy war; a massacre as the murder of many; and heresy as a fundamental error in religion.
webster_full: DUALIST, n. One who maintains the existence of two distinct principles or gods, one good and the other evil.
CRUSADE, n. A military expedition undertaken by Christians for the recovery of the Holy Land from the infidels.
MASSACRE, n. The murder of an individual, or the slaughter of numbers of human beings, with circumstances of cruelty.
HERESY, n. A fundamental error in religion, or an error of opinion respecting some fundamental doctrine of religion.
INQUISITION, n. In Catholic countries, a court or tribunal established for the examination and punishment of heretics.
scriptures: All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
Zec 4:6
Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the LORD unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.
Joh 8:32
And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.
Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
corruption_summary: Languedoc see that named the Albigensian Cathars, whose fortress cathedral of brick was begun in 1282 after the crusade against them.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that two things can be condemned at once. Cathar dualism rejected the Old Testament and the incarnation, and it falls to the claim Paul makes for the whole canon, “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16). They were not proto-Protestants, and the dictionary will not borrow them.

The live temptation is to let the heresy excuse the crusade, or the crusade sanctify the heresy. Neither follows. Zechariah excludes the method outright, “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6), and Christ names the only liberator, “ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free” (Joh 8:32). The duty that remained was argument, “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3), and twenty years of war was not that.

pos: n. (the Quercy see in a loop of the Lot, birthplace of Pope John XXII)
etymology: From the Gaulish tribe the Cadurci, through Latin Cadurcum.
biblical_def: Cahors sits in a tight loop of the river Lot in Quercy, defended by the fortified Pont Valentre of the fourteenth century, and was a see from the fourth. Jacques Dueze, born at Cahors about 1244, became Pope John XXII in 1316 and reigned from Avignon for eighteen years; he reorganised the papal finances with lasting effect, condemned the Franciscan Spirituals over the poverty of Christ, and held and then retracted an opinion that the souls of the blessed do not enjoy the vision of God before the general judgment. He founded a university in his home town in 1331. The dictionary records Cahors for John XXII's financial reorganisation, because it is the taproot of the abuse that provoked 1517. The systematic monetising of annates, reservations and dispensations under Avignon created the machinery that later sold indulgences in Germany, and the sentence that destroyed it was already in the text: “by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves” (Eph 2:8) with “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9), since nothing that may be bought is grace at all.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an annate as the first year's profits of a benefice; a dispensation as the relaxing of a law; simony as the buying or selling of church preferment; an indulgence as remission of penance; and traffic as trade.
webster_full: ANNATES, n. The first year's profits of an ecclesiastical benefice, paid to the pope on the appointment of a bishop.
DISPENSATION, n. The granting of a license, or the license itself, to do what is forbidden by laws or canons.
SIMONY, n. The crime of buying or selling ecclesiastical preferment, or of corruptly presenting to a benefice.
INDULGENCE, n. In the Romish church, remission of the penalty due to sins, granted by the pope.
TRAFFIC, n. Trade; commerce, either by barter or by buying and selling.

corruption_summary: Quercy see and birthplace of Pope John XXII, whose reorganisation of papal finance at Avignon built the machinery later used to sell indulgences.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that grace and price are mutually exclusive terms. John XXII's fiscal system made spiritual benefits into revenue, and Paul's definition rules that out by construction: “by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves” (Eph 2:8). The clause that follows is there precisely to stop the evasion, “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (Eph 2:9).

The live temptation is to treat the Avignon financing as administrative housekeeping rather than doctrine. It was doctrine in practice, and it taught Europe that standing with God could be purchased, against “a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ” (Gal 2:16). Paul's warning covers the apparatus that grew around it, “Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men” (Col 2:8).
